stories.headline: Mamdani releases detailed plan to close Rikers by 2032 with four borough jails
stories.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani on Friday laid out how he intends to close the Rikers Island jail complex by the end of 2032: replace it with four smaller jails around the city and sharply reduce the number of people held. He acknowledged the city will miss the 2027 closure deadline now in law. The later deadline needs City Council approval, according to local reports.
stories.why_it_matters: The plan decides where people awaiting trial will be held, means new jails in four boroughs, and depends on holding far fewer people than the city does today. Outlets across the spectrum covered it; right-leaning outlets focused on releases, others on the missed deadline.
stories.background: Rikers Island is the city's main jail complex, holding more than 6,000 people, most of them awaiting trial. In 2019 the City Council voted to close it and replace it with smaller jails in the boroughs, and the law set a 2027 deadline. Construction delays and a jail population larger than the new buildings can hold put that date out of reach. Mamdani, who took office in January, had already proposed moving the deadline to the end of 2032; Friday's announcement set out the steps to get there. The Council, led by Speaker Julie Menin, must approve the new date.

facts.text: Mamdani announced a plan Friday to close Rikers Island by 2032.
The plan would replace Rikers with four smaller jails across the city.
The mayor acknowledged the city will miss the legal deadline to close Rikers by next year.
The plan relies on sharply reducing the jail population and keeping it down, Gothamist reported.
Rikers holds more than 6,000 people.
The City Council first voted to close Rikers in 2019, and delays followed over where to hold detainees.
The mayor's office described the document as the city's first comprehensive plan to close Rikers.
Moving the deadline from 2027 to the end of 2032 requires City Council approval, ABC7 reported.
Council Member Tiffany Caban, whose district includes Rikers Island, told City & State there is 'a long way to go'.

stories.headline: City closes its last migrant shelter and tells judge ICE subpoena is moot
stories.summary: Lawyers for the Mamdani administration told a federal judge late Thursday that no residents remain at the Bruckner migrant shelter in the Bronx, the site whose resident records Immigration and Customs Enforcement had subpoenaed. The city argues the closure makes the subpoena irrelevant. Reports seen so far do not say how the judge or ICE has responded.
stories.why_it_matters: The case tests how far the federal government can go in getting city-held data about people living in shelters, and ICE has other subpoenas pending for other city-run shelters. The ingested coverage comes from left-leaning outlets only.
stories.background: During the migrant influx that began in 2022 the city opened emergency shelters; the Bruckner site in Mott Haven was the last one still open. The Mamdani administration published a plan in February to close it by the end of the year. ICE subpoenaed the city for information on residents there, and the city fought the request in court. Earlier this month U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan ordered the city to hand over names and dates of birth of certain male residents. The city then emptied and closed the shelter before the data changed hands, according to the court letter described in news reports.

facts.text: Attorneys for the administration filed a letter late Thursday telling a judge there were no more residents inside the Bronx facility.
The shelter was the city's last remaining migrant shelter.
The Trump administration had sought the names of undocumented immigrants with criminal records who lived at the center, according to the New York Times.

U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan had ordered the city to comply with the ICE subpoena for information on male residents of the Bruckner shelter; the NAACP Legal Defense Fund, which criticized the order, dated it to Nov. 6 and said it covered names and dates of birth.
After the ruling, a mayoral spokesperson said the city was evaluating its next steps.
The closure leaves the subpoena's status unresolved, and a wider dispute over shelter data continues, according to the New York Times headline and a Latin Times report.

stories.headline: Council presses Fire Department on battery fires and wants trade-in program back
stories.summary: At a City Council hearing Friday, Fire Department officials defended the Mamdani administration's response to fires caused by lithium-ion batteries, which power many e-bikes. Council Speaker Julie Menin called for reviving a battery trade-in pilot that has expired, and the Council is weighing bills to restrict the sale of uncertified batteries. A relative of a family killed in a Bronx e-bike fire also called for change.
stories.why_it_matters: Battery fires start in apartments and can kill neighbors as well as the owner; what the Council passes will decide which batteries can be sold and whether riders get help replacing unsafe ones.
stories.background: Lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes and scooters can ignite and burn very fast, especially cheap ones that have not been safety-certified. Many delivery workers rely on them. The Council passed a package of battery laws in 2023, including a trade-in program that let people swap unsafe batteries for certified ones; the program ran as a pilot and has since lapsed. Fatal fires this year, including one in the Bronx that killed members of one family, prompted Friday's hearing. The key players are Speaker Julie Menin, the Fire Department and the Department of Transportation, which ran the trade-in pilot.

facts.text: The Council is debating a set of bills to tighten safety rules and limit the sale and distribution of uncertified lithium-ion batteries.
Fire Department officials told the Council they supported the battery trade-in pilot, which has expired; Speaker Julie Menin said the city should bring it back.
Administration officials defended their response to the fires at the hearing.
A relative of a family killed in a Bronx e-bike fire called for change, the New York Post reported.
Menin said the Department of Transportation had failed to extend the trade-in program and called on the mayor to fix that, Streetsblog reported.

stories.headline: Amazon's campaign against delivery worker bill is straining ties with Council speaker
stories.summary: Gothamist reports that Council Speaker Julie Menin is growing frustrated with Amazon as the company steps up lobbying against a Council bill covering delivery workers who work for its contractors. Amazon this week began warning customers in its app that the bill could raise order costs. Other reports say lawmakers are weighing changes to the bill, with a vote possible in the coming weeks.
stories.why_it_matters: The bill would change how thousands of package delivery workers in the city are employed, and Amazon says it could make orders cost more, a claim the speaker rejects. Only Gothamist among ingested outlets covered this today.
stories.background: Many drivers who deliver Amazon packages wear its branding but are employed by smaller contractor firms. The Delivery Protection Act, a Council bill backed by the Teamsters union and Mayor Zohran Mamdani, would regulate that arrangement and the warehouses packages leave from. Amazon opposes it; earlier reporting by New York Focus said the company funded a multimillion-dollar lobbying campaign against it. Speaker Julie Menin controls whether and when the bill gets a vote and has said she is working through legal issues with it.

stories.headline: Bronx funeral held for Javits Frimpong, 15, as prosecutors describe the shooting
stories.summary: A large crowd, including Mayor Zohran Mamdani, attended the funeral Friday of Javits Frimpong, the 15-year-old shot dead on his way to school in the Bronx last month. The Rev. Al Sharpton gave the eulogy. Prosecutors said the teens who killed him took turns shooting, the Daily News reported; one 17-year-old has been charged and police have said they are looking for two others.
stories.why_it_matters: The killing of a student walking to school has become a focus of the city's debate over youth gun violence, and two suspects have not been arrested. Ingested coverage is from left-leaning and center outlets only.
stories.background: Javits Frimpong, a 10th grader who had come from Ghana, was shot on Oct. 29 while walking to school in the Bronx. Police arrested a 17-year-old in November and charged him with murder; the Bronx district attorney's office is prosecuting. The family is represented by civil rights attorney Ben Crump and has been supported by Sharpton's National Action Network. Early reports linked the shooting to bullying, but Crump has said prosecutors told the family the shooters did not attend Frimpong's school; amNY describes the killing as a case of mistaken identity.

stories.headline: Group files new petitions to open city primaries to all voters
stories.summary: Unite NY, a group that wants every registered voter to be able to vote in city primaries, has submitted a second batch of petitions to put the question on the ballot, Gothamist reports. Its first batch was rejected by the city and is still in court. Mayor Zohran Mamdani has pushed back on the effort.
stories.why_it_matters: Voters not enrolled in a party cannot vote in the primaries that usually decide who wins city offices; a ballot question could change that for the next mayoral election. Only Gothamist among ingested outlets covered this.
stories.background: New York City has closed primaries: only voters registered with a party can vote in that party's primary. Because Democrats far outnumber Republicans in the city, the Democratic primary often decides the winner. Unite NY is using a petition process to try to put a charter change on the ballot instead of going through a mayor-appointed charter revision commission. It filed about 45,000 signatures in July; the city clerk found too few were valid, and the group sued. Mamdani has said he is content with the current primary system.

facts.text: Unite NY is trying again to put a question on the ballot opening the city's primaries to all registered voters.
The group's first batch of petitions is still tied up in a legal fight with the city.
The city rejected the first batch, filed in July, saying it fell short of the 30,000 valid signatures required; Unite NY disputes the count and sued.
Mamdani has said he is content with the city's current primary system.
